name: Curved and Angular Living Rooms
description: Method replication: the four images are the paper's own views of its virtual living rooms, shown as still pictures instead of being explored in virtual reality. Two pairs of furnished living rooms (4.9 x 3.9 x 3 m, green as main colour, a window onto a natural view) differ only in contour, angular or curved windows, furniture, fixtures and patterns, within two styles, modern (minimal) and classic (neo-classical furniture, plants and plant pictures): AM angular modern, CM curved modern, AC angular classic, CC curved classic. Participants first report their momentary affective state, are then randomly assigned to one of the paper's four counterbalanced room orders (A: AM, AC, CM, CC; B: AC, CM, CC, AM; C: CM, CC, AM, AC; D: CC, AM, AC, CM), look at each room for 60 s and, with the picture still visible, rate it on the paper's 20 affective and spatial experience pairs (ASE, -5 to +5 between two adjectives such as unpleasant - pleasant, narrow - spacious, chaotic - ordered), the 11 momentary affective state scales (MAS: six 0-10 intensity scales from little to too much and five bipolar -5 to +5 scales) and the 12 Perceived Restorativeness Scale items (0 = not true at all to 4 = absolutely true). Age and gender are asked at the end. Rebuilt from Tawil, Sztuka, Pohlmann, Sudimac & Kühn (2021), The Living Space: Psychological Well-Being and Mental Health in Response to Interiors Presented in Virtual Reality, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 18(23): 12510, with the images cropped from its Figure 1 and all scale items and anchors from its Supplementary Tables S1-S3 (CC BY 4.0). Image ids: AM, CM, AC, CC; group records the room order. Analysis as in the paper: paired t-tests (or Wilcoxon) of angular vs curved and modern vs classic rooms on each ASE and MAS dimension and the PRS total, with false-discovery correction and Bayes factors; the paper (42 participants) found almost no contour effects, only angular rooms rated more novel and more ordered (curved slightly more exciting and harmonious before correction), and the style contrast mainly showed modern rooms as more novel (simpler, more ordered, more spacious and colder than classic rooms before correction). Differences from the original study: (1) still images (overview perspectives that, as the paper notes, do not represent a human eye view) instead of 3 min of free exploration in a photorealistic VR headset with a physical couch, and no virtual training room; (2) the 2-min skip-counting cognitive task, the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire and the presence questionnaire are not included; (3) the 60 s viewing time, the question stems and the order ASE - MAS - PRS after each room are ours; the paper asked the PRS in the post-VR computer questionnaire; (4) the paper used German translations; the English item wording is the one given in the supplement; (5) the age and gender questions are ours; the paper's sample was 18-40 years, mostly born in Germany.
author: Tawil, Sztuka, Pohlmann, Sudimac & Kühn

elements.name: prs

rows.text: There are a lot to explore and discover here.
A lot of interesting things get my attention here.
The things and processes that I observed here are in natural harmony.
To be here corresponds to my personal inclinations.
It is easy to do what I want here.
This place is a world of its own.
Everything seems to have its place here.
When I stay here, nothing unwanted disturbs my concentration.
Spending time here creates a welcome change from my daily routine.
In this place the order of things is easy to see.

elements.title: How true are these statements about this room?
elements.description: Perceived Restorativeness Scale, 0 = not true at all, 4 = absolutely true. Row ids give the original subscale (fa fascination, coh coherence, com compatibility, sco scope, ba being away). Keyed by room id.
